title: Are crickets the future of food?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a personal story about a carbon monoxide alarm going off at Josh's house during basement concrete-cutting work, then turn to cricket farming as a protein source. They cover rising global meat consumption and its resource costs (water, greenhouse gases, cropland used for feed), Kevin Bachhuber's Youngstown, Ohio cricket farm and its FDA approval, the 2013 UN report on edible insects, why Western cultures developed disgust toward eating insects, cricket nutrition and feed efficiency compared with cattle, shellfish chitin, the farming process (egg cartons, heat, humidity, freezing for harvest), home cricket kits, cooking tips, and vegetarian views on eating insects. The episode ends with a listener mail about Kevin Spacey's accent in House of Cards.
topics: vegetarian and vegan views on insects

United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization

segments.title: Opening banter and carbon monoxide scare
segments.summary: The hosts joke about a visitor and a Step Brothers photo, then Josh describes a gas-powered concrete saw in his basement that set off his carbon monoxide alarm while his pets were inside. Chuck says he looks healthy and they tease a cricket sound effect as a segue to the topic.

segments.title: Meat consumption and resource use
segments.summary: The hosts introduce crickets as a possible alternative protein. They cite a doubling of per-capita meat consumption in the developed world over thirty years, driven by BRIC countries' growing wealth. They describe the water needed per pound of beef, the share of greenhouse gases tied to animal agriculture, and the cropland used to grow animal feed versus human food.

segments.title: Kevin Bachhuber and the US cricket industry
segments.summary: The hosts describe Kevin Bachhuber, who tasted fried crickets in Thailand in 2007 and began a commercial cricket farm in the US. They note Thailand's government cricket program, that the US cricket industry previously raised crickets as feed for fish, reptiles and livestock, and that Bachhuber's company was the first approved by the FDA to sell crickets as human food.

segments.title: Why Westerners avoid eating insects
segments.summary: The hosts note that insects are a regular food for much of the world, and that Western countries are among the few that do not eat them. One explanation given is that Eurasian domesticated animals supplied food so insects were not needed, and that a sedentary farming life made insects pests. The resulting disgust is learned and can be unlearned.

segments.title: UN 2013 edible insects report
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a UN Food and Agriculture Organization report on edible insects that promoted insects for nutrition, sustainability and economic viability. Crickets feature prominently. The hosts say the report got wide press and that Bachhuber's US startup followed it, and they question the claim that it was the UN's most popular document.

segments.title: Cricket nutrition and feed efficiency
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the protein, fat, zinc, iron and calcium in insects, and compare feed conversion: crickets need about 1.7 kg of feed per kg of live weight, versus about 10 kg for beef. They explain that crickets are cold-blooded and that their edible share is high. They note that mealworms may be more efficient and mention the idea of insect waste conversion.

segments.title: Shellfish, chitin and allergies
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss chitin, the exoskeleton material in insects and crustaceans, and its supposed health benefits, noting one study showed only a small effect near placebo. They talk about eating whole crickets, soft-shell crabs and shrimp dishes, and Josh recounts overcoming a shrimp allergy through immunotherapy. Chuck recalls declining to eat fried locusts on a Science Channel shoot because of possible allergy, and the UN report says insect allergies are rare.

segments.title: Cricket farming process and home kits
segments.summary: The hosts describe the roughly seven-week cricket life cycle, egg cartons as housing, feed of organic grain, fruit and vegetables, and warm, humid conditions. They explain the two-terrarium home setup for laying and hatching eggs. Harvest is done by chilling crickets into torpor then freezing them. They mention startups selling home cricket kits and the appeal of home farming as side income.

segments.title: Cooking crickets, vegetarian views, and Chirps
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how crickets taste, cite Aristotle's remarks on cicadas, and consider whether vegetarians and vegans accept eating insects, with views ranging from acceptable to not. They discuss Chirps on Shark Tank and cooking crickets, with Daniella Martin's Girl Meets Bug recommending butter, onion and salt, or oven-roasting with olive oil and garlic. They also raise the problem of feeding crickets food waste and the rules that limit it.
topics: vegetarian and vegan views on insects

segments.title: Cricket nutrition facts
segments.summary: The hosts cite Popular Science figures for 100 grams of crickets: about 120 calories, 5.5 grams of carbohydrates, 12.9 grams of protein, 75.8 milligrams of calcium and 9.5 milligrams of iron, or about twenty crickets.

segments.title: Listener mail: Kevin Spacey's accent
segments.summary: A listener named Mary Jean Murphy argues that Kevin Spacey's accent as Frank Underwood in House of Cards fits a character who left a poor South Carolina background for Charleston's old-money style. She describes her own brother training out her accent. The episode includes a House of Cards spoiler warning. The hosts close with social media and website information.
